items.title: feat(cron): per-job toolset scoping + creator user_id in origin

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Context

Hermes's `cronjob` tool is great for persistent scheduled agent sessions, but two gaps make it hard to expose cron creation to anyone beyond the trusted admins of a deployment.

I'm building a bot where allowlisted non-admin users can schedule recurring reports, data queries, and read-only checks — all backed by `cronjob`. After reading the source (v0.9.0), I've hit two blockers that force narrowing to admin-only. Filing in case other Hermes users want the same capability.

## Gap 1 — Per-job toolset scoping

**Current behavior** (`cron/scheduler.py`): every fired cronjob session is initialized with a hardcoded `disabled_toolsets=["cronjob", "messaging", "clarify"]`. No per-job override at creation time. Fired sessions inherit the full `_HERMES_CORE_TOOLS` minus those three — including `terminal`, `process`, `execute_code`, `delegate_task`, file writes, `web_*`, all `browser_*`, `vision_analyze`, `image_generate`, etc.

**Why it matters**: when a cron's creator isn't fully trusted to use every one of those tools, there's no native way to restrict the fired session. A prompt-level constraint isn't a hard gate — the LLM can disregard it under adversarial input, and a malicious prompt can override it.

**Proposed API**: accept an optional `toolsets` (or `enabled_toolsets` / `disabled_toolsets`) parameter on `cronjob(action="create")`. Persist it in `jobs.json`. At fire time, merge with the existing hardcoded disable list so `cronjob`/`messaging`/`clarify` remain off regardless of caller-supplied value (recursion protection stays intact).

```python
cronjob(
    action="create",
    prompt="...",
    schedule="0 9 * * *",
    deliver={"platform": "slack", "chat_id": "..."},
    toolsets=["web", "files", "memory"],   # <-- new
)
```

## Gap 2 — Creator user_id in job metadata

**Current behavior**: the `origin` dict stored with each job records `platform`, `chat_id`, `thread_id`, and optional `chat_name`. It does not record the `user_id` of the person who invoked the create action.

**Why it matters**: when the fired session needs to know *who* created it — for audit, for failure-notification DMs back to the creator, for destination enforcement, or for per-creator authorization checks — there's no trusted source. Putting the creator ID in the prompt text is adversarially editable. A dedicated metadata field is the obvious fix.

**Proposed change**: add `user_id` (platform-specific identifier, matching whatever the gateway surfaces — e.g., Slack `U…`, Telegram numeric chat member ID) to the `origin` dict, populated automatically from the invoking session's context.

```json
{
  "origin": {
    "platform": "slack",
    "chat_id": "Cxxxxxxxxxx",
    "thread_id": "1234567890.123456",
    "chat_name": "#example",
    "user_id": "Uxxxxxxxxxx"
  }
}
```

## Impact

With both fields:
- A deployment can expose `cronjob` creation to a broader user set while still enforcing capability boundaries per creator.
- Fired sessions can resolve creator identity without relying on prompt text.
- Audit logs can attribute every job to a real user from trusted metadata.

Without them, deployments either stay admin-only on cron creation, or maintain parallel state externally — which is what I'll do in the meantime, but it feels like something worth having in Hermes itself.

## Related

- #8616 (`messaging` toolset missing from `CONFIGURABLE_TOOLSETS`) — separate bug but overlaps with the "what toolsets are actually live in a fired session" territory.

Happy to iterate on the proposed API if maintainers prefer a different shape. Both gaps are independent — either is valuable on its own.

items.title: /model silently routes to OpenRouter for direct providers (minimax-cn, zai, etc.)
items.body:
## Bug Description

`/model <name>` (without `--provider`) silently routes models to **OpenRouter** instead of the user's configured direct provider, even when valid credentials exist for the direct provider.

This affects all providers configured as direct connections (minimax-cn, zai, kimi-coding-cn, etc.) — any provider not named `openrouter` or `nous`.

## Reproduction Steps

### Scenario A: Model name matches a direct provider but gets hijacked by OpenRouter

```bash
# Config: MINIMAX_CN_API_KEY is set in .env, custom_providers has minimax-cn
/model minimax-m2.7
# Expected: MiniMax (minimax-cn), provider: minimax-cn
# Actual:   OpenRouter, provider: openrouter
```

### Scenario B: Model belongs to a different direct provider, gets stuck on current provider

```bash
# Current provider: minimax-cn
/model glm-5-turbo
# Expected: switch to provider zai
# Actual:   stays on minimax-cn (model name passed to MiniMax API → error or garbage)
```

### Scenario C: Session override pollution — once wrong, always wrong

After Scenario A succeeds in routing to OpenRouter, the gateway stores:

```python
_session_model_overrides[session_key] = {"provider": "openrouter", ...}
```

All subsequent `/model` calls use `"openrouter"` as `current_provider`, making the OpenRouter fallback even more likely — a sticky failure.

## Root Cause Analysis

The bug is in `detect_provider_for_model()` in `hermes_cli/models.py` (line ~988). Three compounding issues:

### Bug 1: `vendor/model` format never matches direct provider catalogs

Users naturally type `/model minimax/minimax-m2.7` (copying the aggregator format). Step 1 compares this against the static catalog entries like `"MiniMax-M2.7"` (no vendor prefix) — **never matches**.

**Location**: `models.py:1035-1038`
```python
for pid, models in _PROVIDER_MODELS.items():
    if any(name_lower == m.lower() for m in models):  # "minimax/minimax-m2.7" vs "MiniMax-M2.7"
```

### Bug 2: Credential check does not account for `custom_providers` or `.env`

When a model name IS matched in the catalog (e.g., `minimax` provider hit before `minimax-cn`), the credential check only looks at `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` env vars:

**Location**: `models.py:1043-1055`
```python
pconfig = PROVIDER_REGISTRY.get(direct_match)
for env_var in pconfig.api_key_env_vars:
    if os.getenv(env_var, "").strip():  # Only checks os.environ
```

But `zai` is configured as a `custom_providers` entry with `api_key` directly in `config.yaml` — this check **never finds it**, causing a false "no credentials" verdict.

### Bug 3: No-credential → unconditional OpenRouter fallback

**Location**: `models.py:1060-1063`
```python
# No direct creds — try to find this model on OpenRouter instead
or_slug = _find_openrouter_slug(name)
if or_slug:
    return ("openrouter", or_slug)
```

When Step 1 finds a direct provider match but reports "no creds", the code immediately falls back to OpenRouter without checking:
- `custom_providers` in config.yaml (where zai's key actually lives)
- Sibling providers (e.g., checking `minimax-cn` before falling back when `minimax` has no key)
- `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` base URL inference (minimax-cn's base_url could still work)

### Bug 4 (Design): Static catalog `_PROVIDER_MODELS` is incomplete

Many real model names aren't in the catalog at all:
- `glm-5-turbo` → not in zai's catalog (which lists `glm-5.1`, etc.)
- `minimax-m2.7` → catalog has `MiniMax-M2.7` (case-sensitive, no vendor prefix)

This makes `detect_provider_for_model()` return `None`, leaving `target_provider` unchanged on the current provider — silently wrong.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `16f9d020` (latest main)
- Platform: Gateway (Feishu), also affects CLI
- Config: `zai` and `minimax-cn` as direct providers via `custom_providers` + `PROVIDER_REGISTRY`
- Both providers have valid credentials

## Suggested Fix Direction

1. **Strip vendor prefix** before catalog matching in Step 1: `name_lower.split("/", 1)[-1]`
2. **Check `custom_providers` credentials** in addition to `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` env vars
3. **Check sibling/related providers** before OpenRouter fallback (e.g., `minimax` → try `minimax-cn`)
4. **Case-insensitive catalog matching** for direct providers
5. **Don't pollute session override** when the switch result is questionable (e.g., provider changed to openrouter unexpectedly)

items.title: [Bug]: session context cleanup leaks stale HERMES_SESSION_* env values after clear
items.body:
## Bug Description
`get_session_env()` falls back to `os.environ` whenever the contextvar value is falsy, so after `clear_session_vars()` a stale inherited `HERMES_SESSION_*` value becomes visible again.

Affected files/lines:
- `gateway/session_context.py:110-128`
- `tests/gateway/test_session_env.py:172-192`

## Why this is a bug
Gateway handlers use contextvars to isolate session state between concurrent requests. After cleanup, the session should read as unset unless there was a deliberate previous context value. Instead, `get_session_env()` re-exposes unrelated process-level env state, which can leak the wrong `HERMES_SESSION_KEY`/platform metadata back into subsequent reads.

The current code does:
- read contextvar
- if value is truthy, return it
- otherwise fall back to `os.getenv(...)`

That means an intentionally cleared contextvar is indistinguishable from “never set in this process”.

## Minimal Reproduction
1. `source venv/bin/activate`
2. Run `pytest -q tests/gateway/test_session_env.py -q`
3. Observe `test_set_session_env_includes_session_key` fail:

```text
E AssertionError: assert 'agent:main:slack:group:C0ASHAPU4JG:1776212501.961449' == ''
```

A direct repro is also possible:
- set `os.environ['HERMES_SESSION_KEY'] = 'stale-env-key'`
- call `set_session_vars(session_key='live-context-key')`
- verify `get_session_env('HERMES_SESSION_KEY') == 'live-context-key'`
- call `clear_session_vars(tokens)`
- actual: `get_session_env('HERMES_SESSION_KEY') == 'stale-env-key'`
- expected: `''`

## Expected Behavior
After clearing gateway session context, `get_session_env('HERMES_SESSION_*')` should not resurrect unrelated process env values for the just-cleared session.

## Actual Behavior
A stale `os.environ` value is returned immediately after cleanup.

## Suggested Investigation Direction
Differentiate “unset in this context” from “cleared back to default” when reading contextvars, or avoid falling back to `os.environ` for names that are managed by the gateway request context after explicit setup/clear cycles.

items.title: [Bug]: WeCom callback retries enqueue duplicate inbound messages because MsgId dedup is unused
items.body:
## Bug Description
`WecomCallbackAdapter` defines a per-message dedup cache but never uses it, so retried callback deliveries enqueue the same inbound message multiple times.

Affected files/lines:
- `gateway/platforms/wecom_callback.py:48`
- `gateway/platforms/wecom_callback.py:67-71`
- `gateway/platforms/wecom_callback.py:247-270`

## Why this is a bug
WeCom callback senders retry delivery when acknowledgements are delayed or networking is flaky. `_handle_callback()` currently decrypts the payload, builds an event, and always pushes it onto `_message_queue` without checking whether the same `MsgId` was already seen.

The file already declares:
- `MESSAGE_DEDUP_TTL_SECONDS = 300`
- `self._seen_messages: Dict[str, float] = {}`

…but neither is consulted or updated in `_handle_callback()`.

## Minimal Reproduction
Run this under the repo venv:

```python
from gateway.config import PlatformConfig
from gateway.platforms.wecom_callback import WecomCallbackAdapter

# Stub _decrypt_request() to always return the same XML containing <MsgId>m1</MsgId>
# Call _handle_callback() twice with the same request payload.
```

Observed result from a narrow repro:

```text
statuses 200 200
queue_ids m1 m1
```

So the same inbound message is accepted twice and both copies are queued for downstream processing.

## Expected Behavior
Duplicate callback deliveries with the same `MsgId` inside the dedup window should be acknowledged but not enqueued a second time.

## Actual Behavior
Each retry is treated as a fresh message and queued again.

## Suggested Investigation Direction
Apply the existing dedup cache inside `_handle_callback()` (or replace it with the shared helper already used elsewhere) before queueing the event, keyed by the decrypted message ID.

items.title: [Bug]: MessageDeduplicator TTL never expires unless cache exceeds max_size
items.body:
## Bug Description
`MessageDeduplicator.is_duplicate()` says it is TTL-based, but an entry never expires unless the cache also grows past `max_size`.

Affected files/lines:
- `gateway/platforms/helpers.py:25-57`

## Why this is a bug
The class docstring and method docstring both describe TTL-based deduplication:
- `"TTL-based message deduplication cache"`
- `"Return True if *msg_id* was already seen within the TTL window."`

But the implementation returns `True` for any previously seen ID without checking its age:

```python
if msg_id in self._seen:
    return True
```

Expired entries are only purged later inside:

```python
if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
    cutoff = now - self._ttl
    self._seen = {k: v for k, v in self._seen.items() if v > cutoff}
```

So on normal workloads that stay under `max_size`, old message IDs remain duplicates forever.

## Minimal Reproduction
Run under the repo venv:

```python
import time
from gateway.platforms.helpers import MessageDeduplicator

d = MessageDeduplicator(ttl_seconds=0.01)
print(d.is_duplicate('m1'))
time.sleep(0.03)
print(d.is_duplicate('m1'))
```

Observed output:

```text
first False
after_ttl True
```

## Expected Behavior
After the TTL expires, the same message ID should no longer be considered a duplicate.

## Actual Behavior
The message ID remains permanently deduplicated until the cache exceeds `max_size`.

## Suggested Investigation Direction
Check entry age before returning `True`, and/or prune expired entries on every lookup instead of only during size-based compaction.

items.title: Weixin adapter still rewrites Markdown tables/headers/links instead of preserving native WeChat Markdown rendering
items.body:
## Summary

The Weixin (`gateway/platforms/weixin.py`) adapter still rewrites Markdown before delivery, even though the current WeChat/iLink client can render Markdown tables correctly.

This causes a visible regression in WeChat:
- Markdown tables are converted into pseudo list blocks instead of real tables
- Markdown headings are rewritten (`# Title` -> `【Title】`, `## Title` -> `**Title**`)
- Markdown links are rewritten or stripped depending on the path
- Structured content loses native WeChat Markdown rendering

I verified this in a real Weixin chat: a raw Markdown table renders correctly now, but the adapter pre-processes the content and destroys that structure before sending.

## Root Cause

The bug is in `WeixinAdapter.format_message()`:

- `format_message()` calls `_normalize_markdown_blocks()`
- `_normalize_markdown_blocks()` scans outgoing content and rewrites Markdown aggressively
- Table blocks are detected with `_TABLE_RULE_RE` and converted via `_rewrite_table_block_for_weixin()` into key-value bullet text
- Header lines are rewritten by `_rewrite_headers_for_weixin()`
- Inline markdown links are also rewritten

So the transport layer is not the problem. The outbound API still sends plain `text_item.text`, but if the original Markdown is preserved, the Weixin client is now able to render it natively.

Relevant code paths:
- `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` -> `format_message()`
- `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` -> `_normalize_markdown_blocks()`
- `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` -> `_rewrite_table_block_for_weixin()`
- `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` -> `_rewrite_headers_for_weixin()`
- `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` -> `_send_message()` (`item_list: [{"type": ITEM_TEXT, "text_item": {"text": text}}]`)

## Reproduction

1. Use the Weixin adapter with a connected iLink Bot account
2. Send this content through Hermes:

```markdown
# Markdown Table Test

| Phase | Action | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warm-up | Walk / Bike | 4-5 min |
| Isometric | Knee ISO | 4 x 45s |
```

3. Observe the message in WeChat

### Expected
The table should render as a Markdown table in one coherent message bubble.

### Actual
The adapter rewrites the content before delivery, so WeChat receives list-like pseudo-structured text instead of the original table.

## Proposed Fix

Preserve Markdown in the Weixin adapter instead of rewriting it.

Concretely:

1. Stop converting Markdown tables into bullet/key-value text in `_normalize_markdown_blocks()`
2. Stop rewriting headings (`#`, `##`) into custom plain-text substitutes
3. Preserve inline Markdown links as Markdown
4. Keep code fences untouched
5. Keep chunking logic focused on message integrity only:
   - do not split heading lines into separate bubbles
   - do not split Markdown table lines into multiple bubbles
   - keep the whole Markdown table as one chunk when under the message limit

## Validation

I tested a local patch with these changes and verified:

- raw Markdown tables stay intact in `format_message()`
- Markdown headings stay intact
- Markdown links stay intact
- `_split_text()` keeps a short Markdown table in a single chunk
- `python -m pytest tests/gateway/test_weixin.py -q` passes after updating the expectations

## Why this matters

The previous rewrite logic made sense when Weixin could not render Markdown well. That assumption appears outdated now.

At this point, the formatting layer is degrading the UX instead of protecting it. For utility-style bot output (reports, plans, audits, tables), preserving the original Markdown gives a much better result in WeChat than rewriting it into pseudo-natural chat text.

## Related issues

- #7468
- #7617
- #9612

items.title: Bug: _load_skill_payload rebuilds wrong skill_dir for external skills (from skills.external_dirs)
items.body:
## Summary

`_load_skill_payload()` in `agent/skill_commands.py` reconstructs `skill_dir` using `SKILLS_DIR / Path(skill_path).parent`, which produces a wrong path for external skills registered via `skills.external_dirs`. This causes the agent to be unable to locate and execute skill scripts.

## Affected files / lines

- `agent/skill_commands.py:71-77`
- `tools/skills_tool.py` — `skill_view()` result dict (missing absolute `skill_dir`)

## Root Cause

`skill_view()` returns `path` as a relative path (e.g. `migrate-to-memorylake/SKILL.md`). `_load_skill_payload()` rebuilds the absolute skill directory as:

```python
skill_dir = SKILLS_DIR / Path(skill_path).parent
```

For builtin skills under `~/.hermes/skills/`, this works. For external skills (e.g. a plugin registering skills from `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/plugins/memory/memorylake/skills/`), this produces `~/.hermes/skills/migrate-to-memorylake/` — a directory that does not exist.

Meanwhile, `skill_view()` internally has the correct absolute `skill_dir` (`skill_md.parent`) but does not include it in the returned result dict.

## Impact

1. **`_build_skill_message()`** receives a wrong `skill_dir`, so the fallback file discovery (lines 166-173) silently fails when `linked_files` is empty
2. **SKILL.md content** referencing `{skill_dir}` or `SKILL_DIR` for script paths cannot be resolved by the model — the model has no way to determine the absolute path of external skill scripts
3. The model resorts to guessing paths (`~/.hermes/skills/...`, `~/.hermes/plugins/...`), running `find` commands, or giving up and writing its own replacement script from scratch

## Reproduction

1. Register an external skill directory via plugin or config:
   ```yaml
   skills:
     external_dirs:
       - /path/to/my-plugin/skills
   ```
2. Create a skill with a script: `my-plugin/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md` + `scripts/run.py`
3. SKILL.md references `{skill_dir}/scripts/run.py` or `SKILL_DIR/scripts/run.py`
4. Invoke the skill via `/my-skill` in CLI or gateway
5. Observe: the model cannot locate `scripts/run.py` because `skill_dir` in the message context points to `~/.hermes/skills/my-skill/` (does not exist)

## Suggested Fix

Have `skill_view()` include the absolute `skill_dir` in its result:

```python
result = {
    ...
    "skill_dir": str(skill_dir) if skill_dir else None,
    ...
}
```

Then in `_load_skill_payload()`, prefer it over the reconstructed path:

```python
skill_dir = None
skill_dir_str = loaded_skill.get("skill_dir")
if skill_dir_str:
    skill_dir = Path(skill_dir_str)
elif skill_path:
    skill_dir = SKILLS_DIR / Path(skill_path).parent
```

This also benefits builtin skills — the path is authoritative rather than reconstructed.

## Related Issues

- #8110 — External skills excluded from gateway slash command registration (same category: `SKILLS_DIR`-only assumptions)
- #9949 — `external_dirs` relative path resolution depends on cwd

items.title: [Bug]: Context compression falls back to OpenRouter default model instead of main provider when summary_provider=auto
items.body:
### Bug Description

## Bug Description

When `compression.summary_provider` is set to `"auto"` (the default) and `compression.summary_model` is empty (also the default), the context compression task does NOT reliably use the main provider's model. Instead, it falls back to OpenRouter's hardcoded default model `google/gemini-3-flash-preview`, which causes a 404 error when the user's actual provider (e.g., DashScope/Alibaba Cloud) does not have this model.

This causes the agent to appear "frozen" — compression fails, then enters a 600-second cooldown, and the cycle repeats.

## Root Cause Analysis

Traced the full call chain in `agent/auxiliary_client.py`:

1. `call_llm(task="compression")` is called with no model argument (from `context_compressor.py:415`)
2. `_resolve_task_provider_model("compression", ...)` reads `auxiliary.compression.provider: "auto"` and `compression.summary_model: ""` → returns `("auto", None, None, None)`
3. `_get_cached_client("auto", None)` → `resolve_provider_client("auto", None)` → `_resolve_auto()`
4. `_resolve_auto()` first tries the main provider via `resolve_provider_client(main_provider, main_model)` (line 1140)
5. If the main provider client resolution succeeds, compression uses the main model ✅
6. **BUT** if `resolve_provider_client(main_provider, main_model)` returns `(None, None)` (e.g., `_resolve_custom_runtime()` fails to find credentials, or the custom provider pool is unavailable), `_resolve_auto()` falls through to the aggregator chain → OpenRouter → `google/gemini-3-flash-preview` ❌

The core issue: `_resolve_auto()` (line 1121-1162) is designed as a general fallback chain for auxiliary tasks. For compression, this means it can silently route to a completely different provider with a model that doesn't exist on the user's actual endpoint.

## Reproduction

Config (`~/.hermes/config.yaml`):
```yaml
model:
  default: qwen3.6-plus
  provider: custom
  base_url: https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1
compression:
  summary_provider: auto   # default
  summary_model: ""        # default — comment says "empty = use main configured model"
```

Steps:
1. Start a long conversation that exceeds the compression threshold (50% context usage)
2. The agent attempts context compression
3. `_resolve_auto()` falls back to OpenRouter (main provider resolution failed)
4. OpenRouter's default model `google/gemini-3-flash-preview` is sent to the main endpoint's base_url (or OpenRouter), causing a 404

Error observed:
```
Failed to generate context summary: Error code: 404 - {'error': {'message': 'The model `google/gemini-3-flash-preview` does not exist or you do not have access to it.', 'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'param': None, 'code': 'model_not_found'}}
```

## Expected Behavior

Per the config comment in `hermes_cli/config.py:356`:
```python
"summary_model": "",          # empty = use main configured model
```

When `summary_model` is empty and `summary_provider` is `"auto"`, compression should use the main provider and main model — not fall back to OpenRouter.

## Impact

- Agent appears frozen/unresponsive during long conversations
- 600-second cooldown after each failed compression attempt (`_SUMMARY_FAILURE_COOLDOWN_SECONDS` in `context_compressor.py:436-439`)
- Users on non-OpenRouter providers (DashScope, custom endpoints, etc.) are most affected
- 60+ ReadTimeout errors accumulated in errors.log from repeated failed attempts

## Suggested Fix

In `_resolve_task_provider_model()` (line 1879-1885), when `task == "compression"` and `cfg_provider` is `"auto"` and `cfg_model` is empty, read the main provider and model directly:

```python
if task == "compression" and (not cfg_provider or cfg_provider == "auto"):
    comp = config.get("compression", {}) if isinstance(config, dict) else {}
    if isinstance(comp, dict):
        cfg_provider = comp.get("summary_provider", "").strip() or None
        cfg_model = cfg_model or comp.get("summary_model", "").strip() or None
        # ... existing code ...

# ADD: If still auto with no model, use main provider/model directly
if task == "compression" and cfg_provider == "auto" and not cfg_model:
    from agent.auxiliary_client import _read_main_provider, _read_main_model
    main_prov = _read_main_provider()
    main_mod = _read_main_model()
    if main_prov and main_prov not in ("auto", "openrouter", "nous", ""):
        cfg_provider = main_prov
        cfg_model = main_mod
```

Alternatively, make the compression task's auto-detection mirror the vision auto-detection pattern (line 1581-1616), which correctly prioritizes the main provider before falling back to aggregators.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: latest (commit from April 2026)
- Provider: custom (DashScope international)
- Model: qwen3.6-plus
- OS: macOS (Apple Silicon)
- Python: 3.11


### Steps to Reproduce

## Reproduction

Config (`~/.hermes/config.yaml`):
```yaml
model:
  default: qwen3.6-plus
  provider: custom
  base_url: https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1
compression:
  summary_provider: auto   # default
  summary_model: ""        # default — comment says "empty = use main configured model"
```

Steps:
1. Start a long conversation that exceeds the compression threshold (50% context usage)
2. The agent attempts context compression
3. `_resolve_auto()` falls back to OpenRouter (main provider resolution failed)
4. OpenRouter's default model `google/gemini-3-flash-preview` is sent to the main endpoint's base_url (or OpenRouter), causing a 404

Error observed:
```
Failed to generate context summary: Error code: 404 - {'error': {'message': 'The model `google/gemini-3-flash-preview` does not exist or you do not have access to it.', 'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'param': None, 'code': 'model_not_found'}}
```

### Expected Behavior

## Expected Behavior

Per the config comment in `hermes_cli/config.py:356`:
```python
"summary_model": "",          # empty = use main configured model
```

When `summary_model` is empty and `summary_provider` is `"auto"`, compression should use the main provider and main model — not fall back to OpenRouter.

## Impact

- Agent appears frozen/unresponsive during long conversations

items.title: Agent hangs indefinitely on CLOSE-WAIT when custom provider drops connection mid-response
items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes agent processes hang indefinitely when the custom OpenAI-compatible provider (e.g. LiteLLM proxy) drops a connection mid-response. The process enters CLOSE-WAIT state and never recovers, requiring `kill -9`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes with a custom provider pointing to a local LiteLLM proxy (`http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1`)
2. Start a conversation that triggers a streaming API call
3. Restart or interrupt the LiteLLM proxy while the request is in-flight
4. Observe that the Hermes process hangs indefinitely

## Expected Behavior

Hermes should detect the dead connection and either:
- Raise a timeout/disconnect error and surface it to the user, or
- Automatically reconnect and retry

## Actual Behavior

The process hangs forever in `epoll_wait()` (visible as `ep_poll` in `strace`). The socket enters TCP CLOSE-WAIT — the remote closed its write side, but the httpx async event loop never wakes up because `epoll_wait` does not fire on a socket that received a FIN while no data was buffered.

`ps` output during hang:
```
25000 pts/3    00:03:42 hermes   # stuck in ep_poll
65531 pts/0    00:00:36 hermes   # stuck in ep_poll
```

`ss -tnp` shows both connections in `CLOSE-WAIT` to port 4000.

Only `kill -9` recovers them. Any in-progress session is lost.

## Root Cause Analysis

`run_agent.py` → `_create_openai_client()` creates an `OpenAI(...)` client with:

```python
# agent/anthropic_adapter.py line 257
"timeout": Timeout(timeout=900.0, connect=10.0)
```

The 900s `timeout` is an **httpx read/write inactivity timeout** — it only fires when the kernel reports I/O readiness. A CLOSE-WAIT socket that received FIN but has no buffered data does **not** become readable via epoll until a read is attempted. Since httpx uses async I/O via `epoll_wait`, the timeout timer never starts, and the process blocks forever.

`_cleanup_dead_connections()` (line 4245) correctly probes sockets with `MSG_PEEK | MSG_DONTWAIT` and would detect this — but it only runs at the **start** of `run_conversation()` (line 7817), not during an in-flight API call. Once blocked inside `epoll_wait`, no cleanup code can intervene.

## Proposed Fix

Enable TCP keepalives on the httpx transport so the kernel sends keepalive probes on idle connections. When the remote is gone, the probes fail and the kernel closes the socket, waking `epoll_wait` with an error:

```python
import socket
import httpx

transport = httpx.HTTPTransport(
    socket_options=[
        (socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_KEEPALIVE, 1),
        (socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPIDLE, 30),   # start probes after 30s idle
        (socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPINTVL, 10),  # probe every 10s
        (socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPCNT, 3),     # 3 failed probes = dead
    ]
)
client = OpenAI(..., http_client=httpx.Client(transport=transport))
```

This gives a ~60s worst-case detection window (30 + 3×10) instead of infinite hang. The existing `error_classifier.py` disconnect patterns would then fire correctly.

## Environment

- OS: Linux (Ubuntu)
- Provider: custom OpenAI-compatible (LiteLLM proxy on `127.0.0.1:4000`)
- `api_mode`: `chat_completions`
- Hermes commit: `10494b42`
- httpx version: see `pip show httpx`
- Python: 3.x

## Workaround

Kill hung processes manually:
```bash
kill -9 <pid>
```

The existing `_cleanup_dead_connections()` pre-turn check prevents the *next* message from hanging on a stale socket, but cannot rescue a process already blocked in `epoll_wait`.

items.title: bug: bundled mcporter skill shadows native MCP awareness for general MCP queries
items.body:
## Summary

The bundled `skills/mcp/mcporter` community skill intercepts general MCP queries ("list my configured MCP servers", "what MCP tools do you have?") and routes them to the `mcporter` CLI — which always returns zero results for users whose MCP servers are configured natively in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` via stdio transport.

This makes Hermes appear to have no MCP servers configured when it actually has many.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure one or more MCP servers in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` under `mcp_servers` (stdio transport, the standard setup)
2. Ask Hermes: *"list my configured MCP servers"* or *"what MCP tools do you have available?"*
3. Hermes runs `npx mcporter list --output json`, finds no mcporter-specific config files, and responds: *"You currently have no configured MCP servers"*

## Expected behavior

Hermes answers from its own config/runtime knowledge. The `native-mcp` skill even documents this: Hermes has a built-in MCP client that connects at startup. General MCP queries should be answered natively.

## Actual behavior

The `mcporter` skill’s description (`"list, configure, auth, and call MCP servers/tools directly"`) is broad enough that Hermes selects it over native awareness for any MCP-related question. `mcporter` looks for its own config files (`~/.mcporter/mcporter.json`, `/Users/<user>/config/mcporter.json`) which do not exist in a standard Hermes setup.

## Root cause

The `mcporter` skill description overlaps too heavily with Hermes’s own native MCP capabilities. The skill should only activate when the user **explicitly** requests the `mcporter` CLI tool by name, not for general MCP introspection queries.

Note: `skills/mcp/native-mcp/SKILL.md` already lists `related_skills: [mcporter]`, confirming these are meant to complement each other — but currently mcporter dominates.

## Fix

Narrow the `mcporter` skill’s trigger scope in its description/metadata so it only activates on explicit `mcporter`-specific requests (e.g. "use mcporter to...", "mcporter auth..."), not generic MCP queries. General questions about configured MCP servers should fall through to Hermes’s native handling.

## Environment

- macOS, Hermes gateway with 20+ stdio MCP servers configured
- Skill present in both `hermes-agent/skills/mcp/mcporter/` (bundled) and synced to `~/.hermes/skills/mcp/mcporter/`

items.title: [Feature]: Host-level switch to disable prompt-affecting plugin surfaces
items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Hermes currently has a few plugin surfaces that can directly or indirectly affect what the model sees in context:

- `pre_llm_call`, which can inject extra text into the current turn's user message
- `PluginContext.inject_message(...)`, which can enqueue a new message into the conversation
- and, if merged, my proposed `transform_terminal_output` hook, which would allow a plugin to rewrite foreground terminal tool output before it is appended back as a tool result #10155 

From a host/operator perspective they are a different trust level than observer-style hooks such as request/response telemetry or end-of-turn callbacks.

Right now, the available controls seem fairly coarse:

- disable a plugin entirely by name
- avoid loading project plugins unless `HERMES_ENABLE_PROJECT_PLUGINS` is enabled

What seems to be missing is a host-level policy switch that says, in effect:

- allow plugins to observe
- but do not allow them to inject or rewrite model-visible context

This feels especially relevant for:
- hosted or multi-user deployments
- cautious operators evaluating third-party plugins
- environments that want memory sync / telemetry / lifecycle hooks, but do not want plugins to influence prompts or tool results
- future plugin growth, where more prompt-affecting extension points may be added over time

I think this is a useful defense-in-depth feature even when plugin installation is already trusted, because it gives the host a clearer security boundary.

### Proposed Solution

Add a host-level configuration switch for disabling prompt-affecting plugin surfaces while keeping observer-style hooks available.

At a high level, the behavior would be:

- when the switch is enabled, prompt-affecting plugin surfaces are blocked globally
- specifically, this would include:
  - `pre_llm_call`
  - `PluginContext.inject_message(...)`
  - and, if merged, `transform_terminal_output`
- observer/lifecycle hooks would still work, such as:
  - `pre_api_request`
  - `post_api_request`
  - `post_llm_call`
  - session lifecycle hooks

I think this should be implemented as a surface-level host policy rather than as a per-plugin blocklist. Disabling a whole plugin is already possible today; the missing mode is something closer to “observer-only plugins”.

For the blocked surfaces, I think the most natural behavior would be:

- prompt-affecting hooks are not invoked, and `invoke_hook(...)` returns the normal no-op shape (`[]`)
- `inject_message(...)` becomes a no-op and returns `False`
- Hermes may log that the action was blocked by host policy

I would strongly prefer this to be a coarse host policy rather than a large per-hook matrix. The goal is to give operators a clean “observer-only plugins” mode, not to add a lot of configuration complexity.

I also think it would be useful if this policy was designed to cover future prompt-affecting plugin surfaces by category, rather than only the currently known ones.

### Alternatives Considered

1. Disable plugins entirely
This works, but it is too coarse. Some operators may want plugin telemetry, memory sync, or lifecycle callbacks, while still disallowing prompt injection or tool-result rewriting.

2. Rely only on plugin trust / review
That helps, but it does not provide a host-enforced safety boundary. A host-level policy would still be valuable as defense in depth.

3. Add one config flag per hook or per plugin API surface
This would be more flexible, but I think it is too much surface area for the initial feature. A single “prompt-affecting plugin surfaces: on/off” switch seems more practical.

4. Invoke blocked hooks but ignore their return values
I do not think this is the right boundary. If the host wants these prompt-affecting surfaces disabled, the cleaner behavior is to avoid invoking them at all. Otherwise plugins could still perform side effects through those surfaces even though the host believes they are blocked.

5. Do nothing
This keeps the system simpler, but it leaves a gap between “plugins fully enabled” and “plugins fully disabled”, which seems like an important operational mode for Hermes to support.

### Feature Type

Other

### Scope

Medium (few files, < 300 lines)


items.title: [Bug]: OpenViking viking_add_resource sends local paths directly instead of temp-uploading files
items.body:
## Bug Description

The OpenViking memory provider exposes `viking_add_resource` as accepting a "URL or path", but its implementation sends the provided value directly as `path` to `POST /api/v1/resources`.

This breaks local file ingestion over the OpenViking HTTP server. The server intentionally rejects direct host filesystem paths for HTTP callers and requires local files to be uploaded through `POST /api/v1/resources/temp_upload` first, then referenced via `temp_file_id`.

As a result, if the model follows the tool schema and passes a local path such as `/tmp/foo.md`, `/tmp/foo.json`, or `~/docs/file.pdf`, the tool call fails with a 403 instead of importing the file.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes to use the OpenViking memory provider:

   ```yaml
   memory:
     provider: openviking
   ```

2. Start an OpenViking HTTP server, for example at:

   ```text
   http://127.0.0.1:1933
   ```

3. Create a local file:

   ```bash
   echo "# local test" > /tmp/openviking-local-test.md
   ```

4. Call the Hermes memory tool with a local path:

   ```json
   {
     "url": "/tmp/openviking-local-test.md",
     "reason": "test local resource ingestion"
   }
   ```

5. Observe that Hermes sends this payload to `POST /api/v1/resources`:

   ```json
   {
     "path": "/tmp/openviking-local-test.md",
     "reason": "test local resource ingestion"
   }
   ```

## Expected Behavior

`viking_add_resource` should support the local file/path behavior advertised by its schema.

For an existing local file, Hermes should:

1. Upload the file with multipart form data:

   ```text
   POST /api/v1/resources/temp_upload
   ```

2. Read `result.temp_file_id` from the response.

3. Call `POST /api/v1/resources` with:

   ```json
   {
     "temp_file_id": "upload_....md",
     "reason": "test local resource ingestion"
   }
   ```

For an existing local directory, Hermes should zip the directory first, upload the zip through `temp_upload`, then call `/api/v1/resources` with `temp_file_id`.

Remote URLs should continue to be sent as `path`.

## Actual Behavior

The tool sends local filesystem paths directly as `path`:

```python
payload: Dict[str, Any] = {"path": url}
resp = self._client.post("/api/v1/resources", payload)
```

OpenViking HTTP server rejects this with a structured 403 error because direct host filesystem paths are not allowed over HTTP.

Example server-side behavior:

```text
HTTP 403
status: error
error.code: PERMISSION_DENIED
```

The error message is equivalent to:

```text
HTTP server only accepts remote resource URLs or temp-uploaded files; direct host filesystem paths are not allowed.
```

## Affected Component

- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)
- Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

## Messaging Platform

N/A (CLI only)

## Debug Report

Not available for this report.

Local environment used while investigating:

```text
OS: Linux gaonan 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64 GNU/Linux
Python: 3.11.15
Hermes: Hermes Agent v0.9.0 (2026.4.13)
Commit tested: 1e15f525 on fix-openviking-add-resource-local-upload
```

## Operating System

WSL2 / Linux

## Python Version

3.11.15

## Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.9.0 (2026.4.13)

## Additional Logs / Traceback

The failure path is a 403 from OpenViking server when `/api/v1/resources` receives a local path in the `path` field.

```text
PERMISSION_DENIED: HTTP server only accepts remote resource URLs or temp-uploaded files; direct host filesystem paths are not allowed.
```

## Root Cause Analysis

The Hermes OpenViking plugin schema advertises local path support:

- `plugins/memory/openviking/__init__.py`
- `viking_add_resource`
- `url`: "URL or path of the resource to add."

But the implementation always sends the value as `path`:

```python
payload: Dict[str, Any] = {"path": url}
resp = self._client.post("/api/v1/resources", payload)
```

OpenViking server's HTTP API distinguishes remote resources from local files:

- Remote resources: send `path`
- Local files: upload first via `/api/v1/resources/temp_upload`, then send `temp_file_id`

The server route explicitly validates this contract. Direct local paths are rejected by `require_remote_resource_source()`, while uploaded files are accepted through `temp_file_id`.

There is also a secondary issue: `_VikingClient` currently relies mostly on `raise_for_status()` and does not surface OpenViking's structured `status/error/result` response cleanly in all cases.

## Proposed Fix

Update the Hermes OpenViking provider so `viking_add_resource` follows the OpenViking HTTP protocol:

1. If `url` resolves to an existing local file:
   - upload it with `POST /api/v1/resources/temp_upload`
   - pass returned `temp_file_id` to `POST /api/v1/resources`
   - set `source_name` to the local filename

2. If `url` resolves to an existing local directory:
   - zip the directory into a temporary file
   - upload the zip with `temp_upload`
   - pass returned `temp_file_id` to `/api/v1/resources`
   - clean up the temporary zip
   - set `source_name` to the directory name

3. If `url` is not an existing local path:
   - treat it as a remote resource and send it as `path`
   - let the OpenViking server enforce remote URL validation

4. Parse structured OpenViking error responses so users see useful messages like `PERMISSION_DENIED: ...`.

5. Update the tool schema description to make the protocol accurate:
   - remote URLs go through `path`
   - local files/directories are temp-uploaded first

6. Add tests covering:
   - local file path uses `temp_file_id`
   - remote URL still uses `path`
   - structured server errors are surfaced

## Bug Description

`/resume` can resolve a named session to a stale compression parent instead of the newest continuation child. That reopens the old row even when the logical conversation has already moved forward through one or more compression continuations.

## Why this matters

Compression is supposed to preserve one logical conversation across multiple session rows. If `/resume` lands on the old root instead of the newest continuation, users end up resuming the wrong point in time.

## Expected Behavior

When a named or explicitly selected session has continuation children created by compression, `/resume` should follow that chain and resume the newest continuation row by default.

## Actual Behavior

Resolution can stop at the stale parent row, so the resumed session is behind the real conversation tip.

## Suggested Direction

- add a helper that follows only compression continuations, not arbitrary branch/delegate children
- use that helper when resolving `/resume` targets by id or title
- when listing named sessions, project compressed roots to their latest continuation before presenting them
- cover gateway and state-db behavior with targeted tests

## Notes

I have a tested local implementation of this behavior, but it is currently entangled with other local `/resume` work and needs a clean upstream port.

items.title: [Integration] jMunch MCP suite — token-efficient code, doc, and data retrieval
items.body:
## Summary

The **jMunch MCP suite** provides three MCP servers that bring token-efficient code intelligence, documentation retrieval, and tabular data analysis to any MCP-compatible agent. Hermes Agent's native MCP client makes integration plug-and-play — just add three entries to `config.yaml`.

## The Three Servers

| Server | PyPI | Tools | Domain |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| **jCodeMunch** | [`jcodemunch-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/jcodemunch-mcp/) | 52 | Code navigation via tree-sitter AST (70+ languages) |
| **jDocMunch** | [`jdocmunch-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/jdocmunch-mcp/) | 13 | Documentation retrieval (Markdown, RST, AsciiDoc, Jupyter, HTML, OpenAPI) |
| **jDataMunch** | [`jdatamunch-mcp`](https://pypi.org/project/jdatamunch-mcp/) | 18 | Tabular data (CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSONL) — SQLite-backed |

All three implement the [jMRI specification](https://github.com/jgravelle/mcp-retrieval-spec) (Apache 2.0) — an open retrieval interface standard.

## Why This Matters for Hermes

Hermes has 40+ built-in tools but no dedicated **code intelligence**, **doc search**, or **data profiling** capability. Agents currently fall back to raw file reads, which wastes tokens and tool calls.

**Benchmarks vs raw file reading:**
- **37x** fewer tokens consumed
- **19.6x** fewer tool calls needed
- **12.4 billion** tokens saved across all jMunch users

## Hermes Configuration

```yaml
# ~/.hermes/config.yaml
mcp_servers:
  jcodemunch:
    command: "uvx"
    args: ["jcodemunch-mcp"]
  jdocmunch:
    command: "uvx"
    args: ["jdocmunch-mcp"]
  jdatamunch:
    command: "uvx"
    args: ["jdatamunch-mcp"]
```

After restart, tools appear as `mcp_jcodemunch_*`, `mcp_jdocmunch_*`, `mcp_jdatamunch_*`.

## Example Workflow

```
# 1. Index a project
mcp_jcodemunch_index_folder(folder_path="/path/to/project")

# 2. Search for symbols
mcp_jcodemunch_search_symbols(repo="project", query="authentication handler")

# 3. Get precise source code (not the whole file)
mcp_jcodemunch_get_symbol_source(repo="project", symbol_id="src/auth.py::AuthHandler")

# 4. Check impact before editing
mcp_jcodemunch_get_blast_radius(repo="project", symbol_id="src/auth.py::AuthHandler")
```

Every response includes `_meta.tokens_saved` — the agent can report efficiency to the user.

## What I'm Proposing

1. **Optional skill** in `optional-skills/mcp/jmunch/` — teaches the agent the discover-search-retrieve workflow (PR incoming)
2. **Documentation** — add jMunch to recommended MCP servers or community integrations
3. **jMRI as retrieval standard** — the spec defines 4 operations (`discover`, `search`, `retrieve`, `metadata`) that would let Hermes generalize across any retrieval MCP, not just jMunch

## Links

- **jCodeMunch:** [GitHub](https://github.com/jgravelle/jcodemunch-mcp) (1,500+ stars) | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/jcodemunch-mcp/)
- **jDocMunch:** [GitHub](https://github.com/jgravelle/jdocmunch-mcp) | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/jdocmunch-mcp/)
- **jDataMunch:** [GitHub](https://github.com/jgravelle/jdatamunch-mcp) | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/jdatamunch-mcp/)
- **jMRI Spec:** [GitHub](https://github.com/jgravelle/mcp-retrieval-spec) (Apache 2.0)

Happy to iterate on the skill content or config format based on maintainer feedback.

### Bug Description

Bug summary
I’m seeing background process watch-pattern notifications show up in a different Discord thread than the one that originally started the process.

What happened
A background process emitted a watch-pattern match like:

[SYSTEM: Background process proc_xxx matched watch pattern "signal=" ...]


But that notification appeared in my current thread, even though the process was started from a different thread.

So this looks like cross-thread notification leakage / wrong routing.

Why I think this is a bug
From the code path:

tools/process_registry.py puts watch_match events into a global completion_queue
gateway/run.py drains that queue after an agent turn
then it calls _inject_watch_notification(synth_text, event)
_inject_watch_notification() reuses the current event source
so the watch notification can get injected into whichever thread happens to be active when the queue is drained

That means watch_match events are not necessarily routed back to the original thread that created the background process.

Relevant code locations
tools/process_registry.py around watch_match queue insertion
gateway/run.py around:
_format_gateway_process_notification()
queue drain after agent run
_inject_watch_notification()

Observed behavior
Background process started in thread A
Later, while chatting in thread B
watch-pattern notification appears in thread B

Expected behavior
Watch notifications should go back to the original source thread/chat that launched the process
 
or at minimum be filtered by original session/thread metadata before injection

Suggested fix
Either:
include routing metadata (platform, chat_id, thread_id, maybe session_key) directly on watch_match events and route from that
or
only inject drained watch events when they match the current session/thread

Impact
This can leak noisy or confusing system notifications across unrelated threads, especially in Discord.

1. In Discord, start a background process with a watch pattern, for example `watch_patterns=["signal="]`.

The watch-pattern notification appears in the wrong Discord thread instead of the original thread where the process was started.

items.title: Bug: /queue alias q is shadowed by /quit in command registry
items.body:
## Bug Description
`/queue` declares `q` as an alias, but the alias is shadowed by `/quit` because both commands register `q` and the flat lookup keeps the later entry.

### Affected files
- `hermes_cli/commands.py:87-88` — `/queue` declares `aliases=("q",)`
- `hermes_cli/commands.py:163-164` — `/quit` also declares `aliases=("exit", "q")`
- `hermes_cli/commands.py:174-178` — `_build_command_lookup()` overwrites duplicate aliases silently
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_commands.py:97-104` — current test suite codifies `q -> quit`, so the collision is not caught

## Why this is a bug
The registry explicitly advertises `q` as an alias for `/queue`, but in practice `resolve_command("q")` returns `/quit`. That makes one documented alias unusable and causes inconsistent behavior across autocomplete/help/dispatch surfaces built from the registry.

## Minimal reproduction
```bash
cd /Users/genie/.hermes/hermes-agent
source venv/bin/activate
python - <<'PY'
from hermes_cli.commands import resolve_command
print(resolve_command('q').name)
print(resolve_command('/q').name)
PY
```

Actual output:
- `quit`
- `quit`

## Expected Behavior
Each alias should resolve to the command that declares it, or the registry should reject duplicate aliases at import/test time.

## Actual Behavior
The later `/quit` entry overwrites `/queue`'s `q` alias in `_COMMAND_LOOKUP`, so `/q` exits instead of queueing a prompt.

## Suggested investigation direction
- Enforce alias uniqueness when building `COMMAND_REGISTRY` / `_COMMAND_LOOKUP`
- Decide whether `q` should belong to `/queue` or `/quit`
- Update `tests/hermes_cli/test_commands.py` so collisions fail instead of being normalized into expected behavior

## Bug Description
`hermes auth add <provider> --auth-type api_key --api-key ...` still prompts for a label with raw `input()`. In non-interactive environments, that prompt raises `EOFError` instead of falling back to the documented default label.

### Affected files
- `hermes_cli/auth_commands.py:160-163` — computes `default_label`, then unconditionally calls `input()` when `--label` is omitted

## Why this is a bug
The command already has a deterministic fallback label (`api-key-N`), so automation and scripted usage should work without an interactive TTY. Right now the non-interactive path crashes before the credential is added.

## Minimal reproduction
```bash
cd /Users/genie/.hermes/hermes-agent
source venv/bin/activate
python - <<'PY'
from types import SimpleNamespace
from hermes_cli.auth_commands import auth_add_command

auth_add_command(SimpleNamespace(
    provider='openrouter',
    auth_type='api_key',
    api_key='sk-test',
    label='',
))
PY
```

Actual result:
- prints `Label (optional, default: api-key-1):`
- raises `EOFError: EOF when reading a line`

## Expected Behavior
If `--label` is omitted and stdin is non-interactive, the command should use `api-key-N` automatically (or another non-interactive-safe fallback) and proceed.

## Actual Behavior
The command blocks on `input()` and crashes with `EOFError` in non-interactive use.

## Suggested investigation direction
- Gate the label prompt on `sys.stdin.isatty()` (or equivalent)
- Reuse `default_label` automatically when no TTY is available
- Add a regression test covering non-interactive `auth_add_command()` with `label=None/""`

items.title: [Bug]: custom GPT-5 endpoint is forced to codex_responses, ignoring explicit chat_completions
items.body:
## Bug Description

For `provider=custom`, Hermes forces `gpt-5.x` models onto `codex_responses` even when the endpoint is a generic OpenAI-compatible proxy and even when `chat_completions` is explicitly requested.

This makes some custom GPT-5 endpoints effectively unusable in Hermes:
- direct `POST /v1/chat/completions` to the same endpoint works quickly
- `AIAgent.run_conversation()` becomes extremely slow or appears hung
- the runtime can log `Responses create(stream=True) fallback did not emit a terminal response.` before eventually returning

This looks separate from #6209.

- #6209 is about **custom endpoint setup UX** not exposing an `api_mode` choice
- this issue is about **runtime behavior**: even an explicit `chat_completions` choice is overridden later for `custom + gpt-5.x`

## Minimal Reproduction

```python
from run_agent import AIAgent

agent = AIAgent(
    model="gpt-5.4",
    provider="custom",
    base_url="https://<your-openai-compatible-proxy>/v1",
    api_key="<key>",
    api_mode="chat_completions",
    quiet_mode=True,
    persist_session=False,
)

print(agent.api_mode)
# Actual:   codex_responses
# Expected: chat_completions
```

The override happens even though `api_mode="chat_completions"` was passed explicitly.

## Real-World Reproduction

1. Configure Hermes with a custom provider:
   - provider: `custom`
   - model: `gpt-5.4`
   - base_url: `https://<openai-compatible-proxy>/v1`
2. Verify the endpoint itself is fine by calling `/v1/chat/completions` directly.
3. Start a Hermes conversation with the same model.
4. Hermes auto-switches to `codex_responses` because the model name starts with `gpt-5`.
5. The conversation becomes very slow or looks stuck.

## Evidence From Local Testing

Environment:
- hermes-agent commit: `e69526be799edcfa02c25bf8966af2d8cce65ee3`
- version: `v2026.4.13-153-ge69526be`
- provider: `custom`
- model: `gpt-5.4`
- base_url: custom OpenAI-compatible proxy

Observed behavior:
- direct `/v1/chat/completions` to the proxy returned `TESTOK` in about **4.2s**
- `AIAgent.run_conversation()` for the equivalent prompt took about **276s**
- during that run Hermes emitted:
  - `RuntimeError: Responses create(stream=True) fallback did not emit a terminal response.`
- the final answer still arrived eventually, which makes this look like a bad transport/protocol choice rather than a bad API key or bad model name

## Why This Looks Wrong

Hermes docs currently say custom/self-hosted providers work with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint that implements `/v1/chat/completions`.

But in `run_agent.py`, GPT-5 model names trigger a later unconditional upgrade from `chat_completions` to `codex_responses`:

```python
if (
    self.api_mode == "chat_completions"
    and ...
    and (
        self._is_direct_openai_url()
        or self._model_requires_responses_api(self.model)
    )
):
    self.api_mode = "codex_responses"
```

`_model_requires_responses_api()` returns `True` for any model whose normalized name starts with `gpt-5`.

That means the protocol decision is currently driven by the model name alone, even for a generic `custom` provider.

## Expected Behavior

One of these should happen:

1. If `api_mode` was explicitly set to `chat_completions`, Hermes should honor it for `provider=custom`.
2. If auto-detect is in use, Hermes should only auto-upgrade GPT-5 to `codex_responses` for providers/URLs that are known to require it (for example direct OpenAI/Codex-style endpoints), not all custom proxies.
3. At minimum, `custom` providers should not be forced onto `codex_responses` purely because the model name starts with `gpt-5`.

## Actual Behavior

- explicit `chat_completions` is overridden
- `custom + gpt-5.x` is forced to `codex_responses`
- some OpenAI-compatible proxies become extremely slow or appear hung under Hermes even though `/v1/chat/completions` works fine

## Suspected Root Cause

The post-init auto-upgrade in `AIAgent.__init__()` is too aggressive for generic custom endpoints. It treats `gpt-5.x` model names as if they necessarily imply Responses API support and preference, but that is not true for all OpenAI-compatible routers/proxies.

## Suggested Fix

- Honor an explicit `api_mode` override for `provider=custom`
- Restrict the GPT-5 -> `codex_responses` auto-upgrade to direct OpenAI/Codex/OpenRouter-style endpoints that are known to require it
- Or add a stricter provider-family check before applying `_model_requires_responses_api()`

## Related

- #6209 custom endpoint setup should let users choose API protocol (`api_mode`)

### Bug Description

**Hermes version:** v0.9.0 (2026.4.13)

**Authorship:** 
written primarily by Claude but experienced by and reviewed by a human; a human will respond.

## Summary

When `fallback_model` triggers a provider switch, Hermes correctly notifies the user via 
`_emit_status()`, which propagates to Telegram/Discord/etc. When credential pool exhaustion 
causes the *same* provider switch, no notification is sent. The user has no idea they are now 
talking to a different AI.

## Why This Is a Bug (Not a Feature Request)

The notification infrastructure already exists. `_emit_status()` propagates to all gateway 
platforms. The `_try_activate_fallback()` path calls it correctly:



### Steps to Reproduce

items.body:
## Description

The `/model` picker in the TUI shows two entries that both display as "Kimi For Coding":

```
╭─ ⚙ Model Picker — Select Provider ─────────────╮
│                                                │
│   Kimi For Coding (6 models)  ← current        │
│   Kimi For Coding (4 models)                   │
│                                                │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

These correspond to two different providers:
- `kimi-coding` — 6 models (global endpoint, api.kimi.com)
- `kimi-coding-cn` — 4 models (China endpoint)

## Root cause

In `agent/models_dev.py`, both providers map to the same models.dev ID:

```python
PROVIDER_TO_MODELS_DEV = {
    "kimi-coding":    "kimi-for-coding",
    "kimi-coding-cn": "kimi-for-coding",
}
```

In `hermes_cli/model_switch.py` → `detect_available_providers()`, the display name is resolved from models.dev, so both providers get the same `display_name` ("Kimi For Coding"). The `seen_slugs` set only tracks provider slugs, not models.dev IDs or display names, so no deduplication occurs.

## Suggested fix

Track used models.dev IDs or display names in the first loop of `detect_available_providers()` and either:
1. Skip the duplicate entirely if the user only has credentials for one, or
2. Disambiguate the display name (e.g., append "(China)") when a duplicate is detected

Option 2 is preferable since both providers are valid and users may have credentials for both.

## Environment

- hermes-agent 0.9.0
- macOS / zsh

items.title: Discord: /skill group exceeds 8000-byte limit causing CommandSyncFailure on startup
items.body:
## Problem

When the number of installed skills grows large, the `/skill` slash command group payload exceeds Discord's 8000-byte limit per command. This causes `CommandSyncFailure` on every startup, and because the failure is treated as a fatal error, the gateway exits with code 1 — triggering an infinite restart loop via `KeepAlive`.

```
discord.app_commands.errors.CommandSyncFailure: Failed to upload commands to Discord (HTTP status 400, error code 50035)
In group 'skill' defined in module 'gateway.platforms.discord'
  Command exceeds maximum size (8000)
```

Observed with ~95+ installed skills.

## Current workaround

Setting `skill_commands: false` in `discord:` config block skips `/skill` group registration entirely. The basic commands (`/new`, `/reset`, `/stop`, etc.) are unaffected.

## Proposed solution

Replace the boolean `skill_commands` flag with an **allowlist** approach:

```yaml
discord:
  skill_commands:
    - research
    - coding
    - summarize
```

- If `skill_commands` is `false` or empty list → skip `/skill` group entirely (current workaround)
- If `skill_commands` is a list of names → register only those skills in the `/skill` group
- If `skill_commands` is `true` or not set → register all (existing behavior, may hit limit)

This gives users fine-grained control over which skills appear as Discord slash commands without silently hitting the API size limit.

Additionally, the gateway should **not crash** when `CommandSyncFailure` occurs — slash command sync failure is non-fatal and the bot should continue running. The sync failure is already caught in a `try/except` block (logged as WARNING), but upstream in `_run_post_connect_initialization`, so the crash is likely caused by the skill group registration itself raising before sync is attempted.

items.title: [Bug] Anthropic OAuth/Claude Max proxy path can misclassify full Hermes system prompt as extra-usage exhausted

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

Claude subscription/OAuth requests can return:

`HTTP 400: You're out of extra usage. Add more at claude.ai/settings/usage and keep going.`

...even when the Claude auth token is valid and minimal Anthropic Messages requests succeed.

On Tyler's macOS machine, the failure was not caused by the proxy itself, the OAuth token, or tool schemas alone. The trigger was the full Hermes-assembled system prompt on the Anthropic OAuth / Claude Max proxy path.

## Environment

- Hermes repo: `NousResearch/hermes-agent`
- Local branch where workaround was applied: `feat/context-budget-management`
- Local preserving commit: `5eeb76e5`
- Platform: macOS
- Provider runtime:
  - `provider: anthropic`
  - `api_mode: anthropic_messages`
  - `base_url: http://127.0.0.1:18801`
- Auth source: Claude Code / Claude subscription OAuth from `~/.claude/.credentials.json`
- Model: `claude-opus-4-6`

## What we verified

### 1. Proxy and auth were healthy

The local billing proxy on `127.0.0.1:18801` was restored and `/health` returned OK.

A direct minimal Anthropic SDK call through that same proxy succeeded:

```python
client.messages.create(
    model='claude-opus-4-6',
    max_tokens=8,
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Say OK'}],
)
```

Result: `OK`

So this was not simply "proxy down" or "OAuth token invalid".

### 2. The failure was prompt-shape sensitive

Using the same proxy, auth, and model:

- baseline user-only request: works
- Claude Code identity block only: works
- tools only: works
- full Hermes system block: fails with extra-usage 400

A local isolation script showed:

- `baseline` -> OK
- `cc_only` -> OK
- `tools_only` -> OK
- `soul_only` -> extra-usage 400
- `both_system` -> extra-usage 400
- `soul_plus_tools` -> extra-usage 400

Later inspection showed the failing "SOUL block" was actually a ~30k combined system block containing:

- `SOUL.md`
- memory guidance
- session-search guidance
- skill-management guidance
- platform/media instructions
- other prompt-builder text

So the actual trigger is the assembled Hermes system prompt on the OAuth path, not only the profile SOUL file.

### 3. A sanitizer workaround restores local end-to-end success

A local workaround in `agent/anthropic_adapter.py` rewrites several Hermes-specific prompt phrases before sending OAuth Anthropic requests.

After applying that patch, a local end-to-end Skippy turn through the resolved runtime bundle succeeded again:

```text
OK.
```

## Why this should be fixed upstream

This is not just a one-off local profile problem.

Hermes currently injects a large, Hermes-specific system prompt into the Anthropic OAuth / Claude Code path. On at least some Claude subscription / proxy routes, that prompt shape appears to get misclassified server-side as requiring extra usage, even though simple Anthropic Messages requests with the same auth work fine.

That makes the symptom look like a billing/auth outage when it is actually request-shape dependent.

## Proposed direction

At minimum, Hermes should defensively sanitize or slim the system prompt on the Anthropic OAuth path.

Possible fixes:

1. Keep a dedicated OAuth-path sanitizer in `agent/anthropic_adapter.py`
2. Reduce / rewrite the most brittle prompt-builder phrases before they reach the OAuth Anthropic path
3. Add a regression test covering:
   - direct minimal request succeeds
   - assembled system prompt does not regress into known brittle wording
4. Improve logging so this class of failure is distinguishable from genuine exhausted extra-usage state

## Notes

This may be related to the general symptom tracked in #6475, but this issue is narrower and includes a concrete root-cause finding:

- valid OAuth auth
- valid proxy path
- minimal request succeeds
- full Hermes system prompt fails
- sanitizer workaround restores success

items.title: [Bug]: Slack mention prefix (<@botid>) breaks is_command() slash-command detection
items.body:
## Bug Description

`MessageEvent.is_command()` at `gateway/platforms/base.py:693-695` checks `self.text.startswith("/")`. In Slack, when a user addresses the bot with a mention (`<@U0AN0V870R1> /sethome`), the raw event text arrives prefixed with the mention token and fails the `startswith("/")` check — so the command is routed to the agent as ordinary conversational text instead of being handled by the command dispatcher.

In practice: `@Vera /sethome` in a Slack channel is silently ignored as a command; only `/sethome` typed without the mention (DM or plain channel message) actually fires `_handle_set_home_command`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes with Slack adapter, bot installed in a channel
2. In the channel, type `@<bot> /sethome`
3. Observe: nothing happens command-side. The agent receives the message as normal text and typically delegates / replies conversationally.
4. In a DM to the bot (no mention prefix), type `/sethome` — works as expected.

## Expected Behavior

Slash commands should work whether or not the user prefixes with a bot mention. The mention prefix is a natural Slack convention for addressing bots in shared channels and shouldn't silently disable the command path.

## Actual Behavior

`is_command()` returns `False` for `"<@U...> /sethome"` because the text doesn't start with `/`. The message falls through to normal message handling and is delivered to the agent verbatim.

## Root Cause

`gateway/platforms/base.py`:

```python
def is_command(self) -> bool:
    """Check if this is a command message (e.g., /new, /reset)."""
    return self.text.startswith("/")
```

No mention-strip happens before this check.

Note: `gateway/platforms/slack.py:1044` does perform a mention-strip (`text = text.replace(f"<@{bot_uid}>", "").strip()`) but only inside `_handle_message_event` for the normal message path, AFTER the event is already constructed. The MessageEvent reaches `is_command()` via other code paths (e.g., the command dispatch in `run.py:3018-3019` for `/sethome`) with the unstripped text.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

**Option A (preferred):** Strip a leading `<@botid>` token inside `is_command()` / `get_command()` so detection is robust regardless of which code path produces the MessageEvent:

```python
def is_command(self) -> bool:
    text = self.text.lstrip()
    # Strip Slack mention prefix if present (e.g., "<@U0123> /sethome")
    import re
    text = re.sub(r"^<@[A-Z0-9]+>\s*", "", text)
    return text.startswith("/")
```

(and apply the same strip in `get_command()` / `get_command_args()` so the extracted command name is clean).

**Option B:** Normalize `self.text` at MessageEvent construction in `slack.py` — strip mention there, before handing off to dispatch. Risk: other adapters would need their own normalization and drift over time.

## Affected Component

Gateway (base MessageEvent + Slack adapter interaction)

## Messaging Platform

Slack (primarily; any platform that prefixes user messages with a mention token could hit this)

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0 (verified on pod — code at `/opt/hermes/gateway/platforms/base.py:693`)

## Related

- Discord `/sethome` config-write bug: #6447
- WhatsApp `/sethome` persistence: #9220

items.title: [Feature]: Cron job 'created' notification should respect thread_ts of originating message
items.body:
## Problem

When a user in a Slack thread asks the agent to schedule a cron job, the confirmation message Hermes posts ("📁 Cron job created: `<id>` — will run ...") is always top-level in the channel, never a reply in the originating thread. This breaks thread discipline and surfaces internal-looking scheduling chatter at channel top-level where non-participants see it out of context.

## Expected Behavior

If the cron creation was triggered by a message in a thread (`thread_ts` present on the originating MessageEvent), the creation notification should reply in the same thread.

If the cron creation came from a top-level message, DM, or cronjob console, the notification can stay top-level (current behavior).

## Actual Behavior

The built-in "cron job created" notification ignores `thread_ts` and is posted as a top-level message on the channel.

## Context / Motivation

In our deployment the agent operates in shared channels with strict thread discipline (thread-originated requests → thread-only replies). A cron creation triggered from a thread conversation landing top-level is visually indistinguishable from the agent "escaping" the thread for an unauthorized broadcast. It also breaks the common UX expectation that an action taken in a thread reports back in that thread.

Concrete example: a non-owner asked the agent for a weekly digest in a thread; the agent created a cron job, and the "📁 Cron job created..." confirmation landed as a top-level channel message, visible to everyone in the channel rather than scoped to the thread participants.

## Proposed Fix

Wherever the cron creation notification is produced (Slack adapter / cron tool return path), propagate the originating `thread_ts` through to the notification send. Slack's `chat.postMessage` accepts `thread_ts`; the adapter already supports it for other responses.

Signature sketch:

```python
await adapter.send(
    chat_id=source.chat_id,
    text=f"📁 Cron job created: `{job_id}` ...",
    thread_ts=source.thread_ts,   # <-- propagate this
)
```

The same fix likely applies to the "cron job updated" / "cron job deleted" confirmations.

## Affected Component

Gateway — cron tool / Slack adapter notification path

## Messaging Platform

Slack (primarily; Discord thread-like behavior may benefit similarly)

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0

## Related

- #8866 — cron delivery target hijacking (different symptom, same "cron + routing state" family)

items.title: [Feature]: Route Slack reaction_added events to the agent so emoji reactions are observable
items.body:
## Problem

The Slack adapter does not route `reaction_added` (or `reaction_removed`) events to the agent. Hermes **emits** reactions outbound (👀 / ✅ lifecycle ack at `gateway/platforms/slack.py:509-539`, 1131-1138), but it has no code path that consumes inbound reaction events — they fall through to slack_bolt's default unhandled-request handler.

This makes emoji reactions "silent" from the agent's perspective: an operator or owner can ✅ a proposal message, but the agent has no way to observe that, so any prompt-layer rule that treats a ✅ as a confirmation signal is unenforceable without an accompanying text message.

## Expected Behavior

If the Slack app is subscribed to `reaction_added` (already common; required anyway for #6572's suppression fix not to be needed), Hermes should register a handler that converts the event into an internal event/callback the agent can consume — e.g., a `ReactionEvent` that reaches the current session similar to how `MessageEvent` does. At minimum: emit a structured event with the reacting user's Slack user_id, the target message's ts + channel, and the reaction name, so prompt-layer rules and skills can act on it.

## Actual Behavior

`gateway/platforms/slack.py:179-196` registers exactly four Slack Bolt handlers: `message`, `app_mention`, `assistant_thread_started`, `assistant_thread_context_changed`. Nothing listens for `reaction_added`. Grep across the repo confirms no `ReactionEvent` concept exists for Slack (Feishu has `_handle_reaction_event` at `gateway/platforms/feishu.py:1835`, but that's platform-local).

## Use Case / Motivation

We use Slack reactions (specifically ✅) as a lightweight "Owner approved" signal for proposed behavior/config changes. Our prompt-layer rule says a ✅ from an Owner authorizes implementation. Without event routing, that rule is decorative — the agent cannot see the ✅ unless the Owner also posts a text message. We've had to degrade the rule to "✅ only counts if accompanied by a text reference to it," which is awkward UX for Owners used to reacting as a primary signal.

Broader value: reactions are a natural, low-friction confirmation/approval signal in Slack. Many agent-driven workflows (approvals, acknowledgements, snooze/archive commands, "mark as handled") could use them once they're observable.

## Proposed Fix

Add a `reaction_added` (and `reaction_removed`) handler in `gateway/platforms/slack.py` that constructs an internal event and dispatches it to the active session, if any. Shape sketch:

```python
@self._app.event("reaction_added")
async def handle_reaction_added(event, say):
    reaction_event = ReactionEvent(
        platform=Platform.SLACK,
        reaction=event["reaction"],              # e.g. "white_check_mark"
        user_id=event["user"],                   # reacting user's Slack ID
        channel_id=event["item"]["channel"],
        message_ts=event["item"]["ts"],
        timestamp=datetime.fromtimestamp(float(event["event_ts"])),
    )
    await self._dispatch_reaction(reaction_event)
```

Open design questions for maintainers:
- Should reactions on any visible message dispatch, or only reactions on messages the bot itself sent / was mentioned in?
- How should this interact with the existing thread/session routing — tie to the message's thread_ts if the reacted message is in a thread?
- What subset of reactions should trigger agent wake-up vs be logged and ignored?

Happy to help prototype.

## Affected Component

Gateway — Slack adapter

## Messaging Platform

Slack (this issue). A parallel Discord issue may exist — Discord reactions work differently and may already have partial support.

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0

## Related

- #6572 — Slack `reaction_added` generates slack_bolt WARNING spam (proposed fix is a catch-all no-op handler; PR #6580). That fix silences the warnings but explicitly does NOT route events to the agent, so it doesn't address this issue.
- #8372 — configurable reactions toggle (outbound reactions, different angle)
